rv.q: This is a production stuffed with personality, spectacle and wow factor.
It somehow snatches victory from the jaws of defeat.
Unfortunately, the production needs more work and pruning.
This is a noisy, fun show that actually stands head and shoulders above the source material.
It wasn’t always possible to make out the lyrics to the songs, but the ensemble’s sheer energy made amends

Anyway, Burlesque isn’t totally inept, but it’s ultimately just bludgeoning, a clangorous three-hour pantomime on steroids that makes the original film look like a model of tastefully plotted restraint.
The upshot is rambling raunch, musical cliche and automated whooping.
A wonderful night. The principal actors are fantastic. The lights, the music and the stagecraft are masterful.
It's not fabulous, but it's perfectly fine.
An entirely average, run-of-the-mill, engaging evening.
The show aims to dazzle, but too often Rory Beaton’s concert spotlights just blind the audience as they rotate into your eyes in almost every number in Act Two.

The overall effect of this adaptation of the 2010 film of the same name is wearying in the extreme and indicative of the sea change – irreversible, I have a feeling – of a bygone musical era made up of genuine mavericks and the one we inhabit now that exists merely to crib, pastiche, reassemble.
It's bold, it's brash, and it's completely irresistible.

The Burlesque musical does not project the chaos of its production – running at two hours fifty minutes, it feels pacey, high-octane, and often funny, and is more slathered than sprinkled with incredibly eye-catching performances.

Annie, Theatre & Tonic: Burlesque The Musical does feel like a production that has so much potential, but just isn’t quite ready for the West End, at least for those who want to see a musical that is impeccably polished and refined from its book through to the opening curtain. However, it is still a very fun evening out.

Film fans may find Hall’s expanded creative control as director, writer and choreographer both ambitious and distancing from the original emotional core, resulting in a bold reinvention rather than a faithful celebration.
The end result is one of the most fun, camp and frothy displays we’ve enjoyed on the West End in recent memory.
While there is plenty of razzle-dazzle in the athletic dancing and costumes, none of it suggests genuine burlesque in the slightest, whether traditional or modern.

cn.t: Critics are sharply divided on this chaotic musical adaptation, with some hailing it as a camp, high-energy delight and others dismissing it as an overlong, messy disaster that borrows shamelessly from superior sources.
